items.title: Cholera transmission was solved by removing a pump handle
items.claim: In the 1854 Soho outbreak, what did John Snow do?

options.text: He developed the first cholera vaccine
He mapped deaths around Broad Street, identified the public water pump as the source, and persuaded authorities to remove its handle on 8 September 1854

items.reveal:
Snow's spot map of Broad Street showed deaths clustered around one pump. He overruled the dominant 'miasma' (bad air) theory of disease.

The pump handle was removed and cases fell. The cause was a leaking cesspit contaminating the well. Snow published 'On the Mode of Communication of Cholera' in 1855 — but his germ theory was not widely accepted until the 1860s with Pasteur and Koch.

London's main response was Joseph Bazalgette's sewer system (1859-1875), built largely after the 'Great Stink' of 1858 made Parliament unbearable.
items.why: Public health is often credited to grand theories. The 1854 case shows that careful observation and a map could outperform the dominant medical theory of the day — even before the underlying biology was understood.

items.title: Thomas Becket was murdered in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170

options.text: Becket died of natural causes during a service

Four knights of Henry II — Reginald FitzUrse, Hugh de Morville, William de Tracy, Richard le Breton — murdered Archbishop Becket in Canterbury Cathedral after Henry's outburst 'Will no one rid me of this turbulent priest?'
He was executed for treason after a public trial

items.reveal:
Becket and Henry had clashed for years over the jurisdiction of church courts (Constitutions of Clarendon, 1164). Becket had fled to France, returned in 1170, and excommunicated bishops who had supported Henry. The king's exact words are disputed but the four knights took them as licence.

Becket was canonised in 1173. Henry II did public penance at Canterbury in 1174, walking barefoot and being scourged by monks. The shrine became one of medieval Europe's major pilgrimage sites — the setting of Chaucer's 'Canterbury Tales' (1380s).

Henry VIII destroyed the shrine in 1538 during the Dissolution.
items.why: Church-state conflict was the defining political question of high medieval Europe. Becket's murder dramatised the limits of royal power over the church — and made Canterbury a centre of European devotion for 350 years.

items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.
